proposals.name: Removes or inverts a standard default rather than adding to it
proposals.instruction: Score how far the work subtracts from or overturns a component the field currently treats as mandatory, versus appending a component to an accepted pipeline. 10 = the abstract names a specific standard practice and shows it can be dropped, held fixed, or is actively harmful, and that subtraction is itself the contribution. 5 = it modifies a standard component but leaves the surrounding assumption untouched. 0 = it adds a new module, loss, or training stage to an unquestioned pipeline and motivates it purely as an improvement. Judge from what the abstract asserts about the prior default, not from adjectives such as novel.
proposals.rationale: R09 argues the final learned classifier layer can be fixed outright; R24 argues the customary perceptual loss becomes superfluous; R06 removes the requirement that test data be present during training. All three sit in the dense_high_card_low half and none of them carry the surface features (dataset counts, percentage deltas, code links) a written criterion bank most easily rewards, so a scorecard reads them as thin while a reader sees a load-bearing subtraction.

proposals.name: One load-bearing mechanism versus several stacked components
proposals.instruction: Score whether a single identifiable mechanism carries the claimed effect. 10 = exactly one change is proposed, and the abstract makes clear that this change is what produces the reported behaviour. 5 = a main mechanism plus one supporting trick, with the split of credit stated. 0 = three or more separately motivated ingredients are chained (an encoding, plus a generator network, plus an auxiliary objective, plus a training procedure), each described as a contribution, with no statement of which one matters. Do not reward the number of components; reward attributable causality.
proposals.rationale: R57 enumerates three components (population-size encoding, hypernetwork, size as extra input) plus a multi-task training procedure; R39 stacks hyperbolic geometry, self-paced weighting and a self-supervised objective; R30 combines a continuous encoding search space with a designed regularizer. All are dense_low_card_high: a per-criterion bank scores each ingredient as separate evidence of contribution, whereas R49 and R09 each rest on one mechanism and are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Reusable primitive versus application-specific pipeline
proposals.instruction: Score how far the contribution is a self-contained primitive that another researcher could drop into an unrelated system. 10 = the contribution is a single estimator, layer, sampler, optimizer or objective, stated in terms independent of any one dataset, and the abstract indicates it applies across architectures or tasks. 5 = a method that generalizes within one modality. 0 = an end-to-end system engineered for one application domain, whose description cannot be stated without naming that domain. Breadth of benchmark list is not the same as primitive reusability and must not substitute for it.
proposals.rationale: R49 offers a gradient estimator, R47 an optimizer, R06 a sampling scheme; each is stated independently of the task it is demonstrated on and all are dense_high_card_low. R56 (vehicle trajectory with lane occupancy) and R43 (zebrafish swim bout classification) are dense_low_card_high pipelines whose method statement is inseparable from the application, yet they present cleanly against per-criterion checks for motivation, method detail and evaluation.

proposals.name: Delivers an instrument that tests other systems
proposals.instruction: Score whether the contribution is a measuring device (an attack, a verifier, a certification procedure, an evaluation protocol, a diagnostic dataset) whose value lies in what it reveals about other models, rather than a new predictor that scores better. 10 = the paper produces a tool that changes what the field can measure or audit, and states what it reveals. 5 = a method with a substantial diagnostic component. 0 = a predictor evaluated on standard benchmarks with no measurement contribution. Judge from the stated purpose of the artifact in the abstract text only.
proposals.rationale: R07 (meta-gradient attacks on graph neural networks), R28 (exact mixed-integer verification), R17 (black-box attack framework unifying prior work), R32 (a description-length evaluation metric for representations) and R12 (a stealthy backdoor construction) are all dense_high_card_low. Instrument papers report what they expose rather than a win over a baseline, so criteria that look for improvement over prior methods on a benchmark under-credit them systematically.

proposals.name: Explains an existing phenomenon, not only builds a new artifact
proposals.instruction: Score whether the reader ends the abstract believing something different about an object that already exists. 10 = the paper's core output is an explanation or characterisation of a known method or phenomenon (why it works, when it breaks, what it actually computes), and the explanation is specific enough to be wrong. 5 = an artifact accompanied by real analysis of its behaviour. 0 = a new artifact whose only account of itself is that it performs better. Explanation must be about a pre-existing object, not about the paper's own new module.
proposals.rationale: R53 characterises double descent in finite-width networks via the Hessian spectrum; R44 gives a spectral account of what a graph convolution actually filters; R09 changes what is believed about the last layer; R32 reinterprets representation evaluation as model selection. These are dense_high_card_low. Explanatory papers often have no headline number and few released assets, so a bank built around method, experiments and resources scores them low while a reader treats the understanding itself as the result.

proposals.name: Theory is load-bearing: the derivation licenses the method
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the stated theory determines the proposed procedure. 10 = a specific proved statement is what makes the algorithm possible or correct, and the abstract shows the path from the statement to the procedure (an identity that yields a tractable objective, a duality that makes a gradient computable, a proof that one objective equals another). 5 = theory that bounds or justifies a method chosen on other grounds. 0 = formal apparatus, background exposition, or a proof of a property nobody doubted, with the method unchanged if the theory were deleted.
proposals.rationale: R58 proves that the divergence between stochastic processes equals a supremum of finite-marginal divergences and then builds the training objective on exactly that; R42 derives the dual form and shows the gradient is explicitly computable; R34 proves the new search gradient optimises the same objective as the reinforcement-learning formulation. All are dense_high_card_low. R23 (dense_low_card_high) advertises a self-contained overview of algebraic topology and design guidance, which reads as strong theoretical content to a checklist but does not force the method.

proposals.name: Positions against a named strongest prior with a stated inability
proposals.instruction: Score the specificity of the comparison target. 10 = the abstract names the actual leading prior method and states precisely what it cannot do or where it fails, in terms concrete enough that the failure could be checked. 5 = a named family of approaches with a general limitation. 0 = the prior work is referred to only as existing approaches, previous methods, or current techniques, and the limitation is that the paper's own idea has not been tried. Number of baselines counted in the evaluation does not count here; only the named target of the argument does.
proposals.rationale: R47 names the specific layerwise adaptive scheme and states that it performs poorly for attention models; R06 names the originating graph convolution work and gives two concrete structural limits. Both dense_high_card_low. R26 says existing approaches completely ignore solution multiplicity and R08 compares to previous methods that search for successful trajectories; both are dense_low_card_high, and both would pass a related-work-engagement check on the presence of a contrast rather than on its sharpness.

proposals.name: Capability regime change versus incremental resource savings
proposals.instruction: Score whether the efficiency or scale result makes something previously infeasible now possible. 10 = the abstract states a qualitative change of regime (a class of problem now tractable, a scale of model now verifiable, a training run now inside a working day) and names the previous ceiling. 5 = a large constant-factor gain in a widely used setting. 0 = a percentage or small multiple saved on one model in one pipeline, with the feasible set unchanged. Score the change in what is possible, not the size of the printed number.
proposals.rationale: R28 certifies networks with an order of magnitude more nonlinearities than any complete verifier had handled and determines an exact quantity for the first time; R47 turns three days of training into 76 minutes; R06 reports orders-of-magnitude training gains; all dense_high_card_low. R29 (five-fold inference, two-fold latency) and R01 (40 percent embedding compression at 0.5 percent accuracy cost) are dense_low_card_high and present far more quotable numbers per sentence, which is exactly what a numeric-evidence criterion rewards.

proposals.name: Claim scope matched to evidence scope
proposals.instruction: Score the fit between how general the claim is and how general the reported support is. 10 = the abstract states the exact conditions under which the result holds (the assumptions, the regime, the quantity achieved) and claims nothing beyond them. 5 = a moderately general claim with representative support. 0 = the abstract advertises a generic or universal approach, or a new state of the art for an entire problem area, on the strength of results in a bounded setting. Penalise only the mismatch; a narrow claim narrowly supported scores well.
proposals.rationale: R30 and R23 both sell a generic approach to an entire problem class, and R03 claims new state-of-the-art results in hyperparameter optimisation off one reformulation; all three are dense_low_card_high. R27 and R28 (dense_high_card_low) instead state exactly what is achieved and under which assumptions. Scope words such as generic, unified and universal read as ambition to a criterion that asks whether the contribution is significant, while a reader discounts them.

proposals.name: Headline claim survives the abstract's own qualifiers
proposals.instruction: Read the strongest sentence of the abstract, then read the reported details, and score whether the strong sentence still stands. 10 = the lead claim is exactly what the detailed results show; no later sentence narrows it. 5 = the lead claim is broad but the narrowing is stated up front. 0 = a broad superiority claim is made first and later details reduce it to a subset (one dataset out of several, some tasks, comparable or better). Score consistency between claim and detail, not the level of performance.
proposals.rationale: R39 leads on outperforming the state of the art and then reveals it holds on one dataset and two of three downstream tasks; R25 claims superior performance and then settles for comparable or higher sample efficiency; R03 asserts new state of the art after listing benchmark counts. All three are dense_low_card_high: itemised criteria for evaluation breadth and for reporting results credit the counts and the disclosures separately, and never compare the headline against the fine print.

proposals.name: Informative density under brevity, no field-importance preamble
proposals.instruction: Score content per sentence. 10 = every sentence carries mechanism, claim, or evidence, and the abstract begins at the technical problem; a short abstract that fully specifies its idea scores at the top. 5 = one framing sentence followed by substantive content. 0 = several opening sentences asserting the importance of the field or the ubiquity of the application, followed by generic method description. Length is not the target: a long abstract that is dense scores high, and a short abstract that is vague scores low.
proposals.rationale: R37 is three sentences, all of them mechanism and claim; R49, R38 and R09 are similarly compact and specific; all are dense_high_card_low, and R02 has no abstract text at all yet holds mid-rank on the dense side. R29, R08 and R23 (dense_low_card_high) open with two or more sentences on why the application area matters. Criteria that ask whether motivation and context are established reward the preamble and penalise the compact abstracts for missing sections.

proposals.name: Result contradicts a competent reader's prior, with the reason given
proposals.instruction: Score surprise that is earned. 10 = the reported finding runs against what a well-informed reader would have predicted, and the abstract says which expectation is violated and why the mechanism produces the violation. 5 = a finding that is somewhat unexpected but attributed only to the new method being better. 0 = the finding is what anyone would have guessed from the setup (a new component helps on the benchmark it was designed for). The judge must state the violated expectation in one clause; if none can be named, score below 3.
proposals.rationale: R09 finds the last layer need not be trained at all; R07 finds attacked models fall below a baseline that ignores all relational information; R24 finds an auxiliary loss the field had treated as necessary is superfluous. All three are dense_high_card_low. Surprise is not a property any single written criterion asks about, so it is the most likely source of dense-side signal that a bank of independently scored properties cannot recover by summation.

proposals.name: Coins a new problem or name only for a demonstrated phenomenon
proposals.instruction: Score naming discipline. 10 = the paper introduces at most one new term, and the phenomenon or object the term denotes is exhibited in the abstract before it is named. 5 = a method acronym for a real mechanism, with no other coinage. 0 = a new problem, task, or setting is formally defined mainly because the paper wishes to solve it, or multiple sub-components each receive their own name. Judge the ratio of new vocabulary to demonstrated content, not the aesthetics of the name.
proposals.rationale: R05 names a new problem (amalgamating optimizers) on the argument that no single optimizer dominates, then names three mechanisms inside it; R26 formally defines a new task before showing the phenomenon costs anything; R13 introduces a coinage for a representation choice. All dense_low_card_high. R09 and R28 (dense_high_card_low) introduce essentially no new vocabulary. Criteria that check for a clearly defined problem and clearly named contributions actively reward coinage.

proposals.name: Released artifact proportionate to the claim's dependence on it
proposals.instruction: Score the release statement against what the claim needs. 10 = the released object is the contribution or is required to believe it (a hand-built dataset the argument rests on, generators whose outputs are the claimed result). 5 = code released for a method whose claims are reproducible in principle from the description. 0 = a boilerplate availability sentence attached to a result that turns on numbers the reader cannot check either way. A bare repository URL with no stated relation to the claim scores no higher than 4.
proposals.rationale: R14 releases human-revised counterfactual documents that are themselves the object of study and R21 releases the learned perturbation sets and weights that constitute the claim; both dense_high_card_low. R01, R60 and R30 (dense_low_card_high) append a repository link to a percentage improvement. A reproducibility criterion scored 0-10 on the presence of a link gives all of these the same high mark, which inflates precisely the incremental-delta papers.

proposals.name: Mechanism content outweighs promotional vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Count the evaluative self-description (remarkable, significant superiority, novel, extensive experiments, excellent, comprehensive) against the mechanical description of what is actually done. 10 = the abstract describes the mechanism precisely enough to be reimplemented in outline and contains almost no self-praise; results are stated as quantities or as capabilities. 5 = mixed, with real mechanism and routine promotional framing. 0 = repeated superlatives about the method's own performance carrying sentences that contain no mechanism. Do not penalise confident claims that are specific; penalise praise that substitutes for description.
proposals.rationale: R56 (remarkable performance gain), R57 (significant superiority, extensive experiments), R03 and R25 lean on evaluative framing and are dense_low_card_high; R49, R09 and R37 state the mechanism flatly and are dense_high_card_low. Judges scoring criteria such as clarity of contribution and strength of results read superlatives as evidence of both, so promotional density is a plausible route by which the scorecard is over-credited relative to the dense reading.

proposals.name: Sheer expository volume of the abstract body
proposals.instruction: Read only the abstract text and rate 0-10 how much total expository volume is present. Anchors: 0 = title only, or a single sentence of body text; 3 = roughly two to four sentences; 6 = one standard paragraph of about eight to twelve sentences; 10 = a long multi-part abstract of fifteen or more sentences covering several elaborated sub-topics. Count sentences, clauses, enumerated sub-points and number of distinct sub-topics touched. You are measuring QUANTITY OF TEXT ONLY. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is clear or informative, or whether a short abstract is terse-and-confident versus thin. Longer is not better and shorter is not better; report extent only.
proposals.rationale: Any scorecard built from a bank of explicit criteria can only fire on criteria whose evidence is literally written down, so raw token supply mechanically caps the achievable card score while a dense reader is free to price a terse text on its content. The slice shows exactly this asymmetry at both extremes: R06 has no abstract body at all (title only) and sits at card_pct=0.192 against dense_pct=0.521, and R24 is two sentences long with card_pct=0.321 against dense_pct=0.996 - the single largest disagreement in the slice. R27, R34 and R59 are likewise short and land card-low relative to dense. In the opposite direction the longest, most enumerative texts R14 (card 0.923) and R21 (card 0.974) sit far above their dense ranks. Word supply is a writing habit, not research quality.

proposals.name: Density of specific quantified result figures
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of explicitly quantified outcome figures in the text. Count numerals attached to results: percentages, absolute metric values (accuracy, AP, mIoU, FID, MAE), speedup or reduction factors (for example five-fold, two to three orders of magnitude), parameter, FLOP or batch-size counts, wall-clock times, and dataset sizes. Anchors: 0 = no such numerals anywhere; 3 = one figure; 5 = two or three; 8 = four or five; 10 = six or more distinct quantified figures, several carried to one or two decimal places. Score PRESENCE AND DENSITY of numbers only. Do not assess whether the numbers are large, impressive, fairly compared, correctly computed, or whether the gains would matter to anyone.
proposals.rationale: A criterion bank almost always contains items that ask whether results are concrete and quantified, so numeral density converts directly into card score independent of what the numerals mean. R14 carries six percentage figures (40 percent, 0.5 percent, 2.8 percent, 43 percent, 0.8 percent, 3 percent) at card 0.923 versus dense 0.372; R21 reports 10.9 percent and 12.4 percent MAE improvements at card 0.974 versus dense 0.094; R36 stacks 1.6 percent Top-1, 0.16M parameters, 0.07B FLOPs and 3-4 percent AP at card 0.868 versus dense 0.415; R26 quotes 6.12 percent and 96.32 percent at card 0.564 versus dense 0.158. The dense model prices all four far lower. Tagged mixed because genuinely strong empirical work does tend to produce numbers to report, so the parent habit is entangled with real quality and must appear in the undiscounted band too.

proposals.name: Prominence of a coined brandable method name
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how prominently the text brands its contribution with a coined name: an invented acronym or capitalised product-style label that is introduced and then reused as the grammatical subject of later sentences, and that also appears in the title. Anchors: 0 = no coined name anywhere, the contribution is referred to only by descriptive noun phrases such as our method, our bound, our framework; 3 = a name is coined once and never reused; 6 = a name is coined and reused two or three times in the body; 10 = a memorable acronym appears in the title and recurs four or more times as the protagonist of the abstract. Score BRANDING PRACTICE ONLY. Do not judge whether the name is apt, clever, pronounceable, or whether it denotes a substantive contribution.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. Naming a method is a dissemination convention that groups learn from senior mentorship and use to make work quotable; it leaves an unmistakable textual trace and is trivially detectable by a criterion bank containing anything like states a clear named contribution. In the slice the branded texts sit card-high and dense-low: R21 (RLEL, card 0.974 vs dense 0.094), R35 (IRIS, card 0.953 vs dense 0.573), R37 (GPO, card 0.906 vs dense 0.415), R40 (HYSP, card 0.795 vs dense 0.449). The unbranded, descriptively-titled texts sit at the very bottom of the card scale while the dense model is far less negative: R28 (card 0.004 vs dense 0.278), R29 (card 0.030 vs dense 0.474), R02 (card 0.043 vs dense 0.389). Tagged mixed because well-resourced, well-mentored groups plausibly both brand better and do better work.
proposals.upstream_parent: lab branding and dissemination practice (seniority, media habits of the producing group)

proposals.name: Promotional template register and self-applied intensifiers
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of formulaic construction phrases combined with evaluative intensifiers that the authors apply to their own work. Formulaic phrases include: in this work we propose a novel, extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of, achieves state-of-the-art, sheds light on, our contributions are N-fold, to bridge this gap, to the best of our knowledge. Self-applied intensifiers include: remarkable, significant superiority, excellent, surprisingly, by a large margin, comfortably surpasses, ground-breaking, considerable. Anchors: 0 = neutral descriptive prose with none of either; 5 = two or three template phrases and one intensifier; 10 = the abstract is largely assembled from such templates and carries four or more self-applied intensifiers. Score REGISTER AND PHRASE FREQUENCY ONLY. Do not judge whether the claims are warranted, and do not treat plain prose as worse or ornate prose as better.
proposals.rationale: This is a stylistic register that a criterion judge reads as claim strength and confidence, and it is copied wholesale between papers in a community, so it is decoupled from the underlying work. The register is concentrated in the card-favoured half: R51 (remarkable performance gain, state-of-the-art, card 0.910 vs dense 0.517), R36 (Surprisingly, by a large margin, card 0.868 vs dense 0.568), R39 (significant superiority, extensive experiments, card 0.568 vs dense 0.291), R05 (ground-breaking, card 0.603 vs dense 0.056). Critically, the same register also appears in card-LOW rows such as R38 (extensive experiments, sheds light on a general principle, card 0.453) and R23 (extensive experiments are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness, card 0.462), which is exactly what a spurious channel should look like: it moves the readout without tracking anything the dense model finds meaningful.

proposals.name: Defensive pre-emption of anticipated objections
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text pre-empts objections rather than simply describing the work. Count moves of these kinds: an explicit negative concession about the authors own results; a disclaimer that the method is not overfit or not narrow; a statement that a confound, artifact or degenerate solution was found and then removed or guarded against; an assurance of robustness to hyperparameters or of validity of the evaluation; and an itemised First / Second / Third / Fourth or N-fold answer-list that reads as a point-by-point response. Anchors: 0 = purely descriptive, no concessions and no guards; 4 = one such move; 7 = two or three; 10 = four or more distinct defensive moves. Score the PRESENCE OF THE RHETORICAL MOVE ONLY. Never judge whether the defence is convincing, whether the concern it addresses is real, or whether the work is therefore sound.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. Whether a manuscript has already been through a review cycle elsewhere is invisible in the text, but its consequence is not: a revised manuscript accretes concessions, guards and point-by-point structure written to answer specific earlier criticism. That accretion is precisely what a criterion bank containing items on rigour, limitations and thoroughness rewards. The pattern is concentrated in the card-favoured half: R15 states its results demonstrate the approach is not overfit to its target problem and concedes that it underperforms one benchmark in a single game (card 0.406 vs dense 0.132); R26 reports uncovering that the network attended to experimental artifacts and removing them to ensure validity (card 0.564 vs dense 0.158); R50 runs an explicit First / Second / Third / Fourth answer-list (card 0.628 vs dense 0.154); R25 defends against being oblivious to solution multiplicity (card 0.376 vs dense 0.081). Tagged mixed because a real revision cycle can genuinely improve the work as well as the packaging.
proposals.upstream_parent: prior review or resubmission history of the manuscript

proposals.name: Advertised code, model and dataset release
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text advertises released artifacts. Anchors: 0 = no mention of code, models or data availability; 3 = a bare future-tense promise such as codes will be released or we will publicly release both datasets; 6 = a present-tense statement that code is available, without a link; 8 = a full working-looking URL to a repository; 10 = a full URL plus explicit enumeration of code AND models or weights AND data, or an explicit reproducibility statement alongside the link. Score the ADVERTISEMENT AS WRITTEN ONLY. Do not judge whether open release is good practice, whether the artifact would be useful, or whether its presence makes the work more trustworthy.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. Maintaining a public repository at submission time is a function of engineering staffing, legal and institutional clearance and group convention rather than of the ideas; the unseen resource factor leaves a one-line trace that any criterion bank picks up as reproducibility. Six of the thirty card-favoured rows carry a live URL: R21 (card 0.974), R35 (0.953), R36 (0.868), R44 (0.821), R40 (0.795), R58 (0.731) - and the dense model ranks all six far lower. The counterexample matters as much: mere future-tense pledges without a link sit card-LOW, R60 (codes will be released, card 0.423) and R41 (we will publicly release both datasets, card 0.120), so what is being scored is the artefact of infrastructure, not the intent. Tagged mixed because well-resourced engineering groups plausibly also produce better-executed research.
proposals.upstream_parent: engineering support and institutional infrastructure available to the producing group

proposals.name: Reported evaluation breadth and compute footprint
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how large a resource and evaluation footprint the text reports. Count: number of distinct named datasets, benchmarks or task suites; number of named baselines or competitor methods; number of distinct architectures or model families covered; and explicit references to large-scale compute such as TPU pods, very large batch sizes, GPU memory budgets, multi-day training runs, or industrial-scale corpora. Anchors: 0 = no dataset, baseline or scale mentioned at all; 3 = a single dataset or benchmark; 5 = two or three datasets; 8 = four or more datasets or an explicit benchmark suite plus several baselines; 10 = a sweeping protocol (many suites, a large enumerated baseline count) or explicitly industrial-scale hardware. Count WHAT IS REPORTED ONLY. Do not judge whether the evaluation is adequate, appropriate, well-chosen or convincing, and do not penalise a purely theoretical text for having nothing to count - score it 0 without prejudice.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. Compute budget and headcount are unobservable but leave a very loud trace: the number of benchmarks a group can afford to run and the hardware it can name. A criterion bank scoring evaluation thoroughness reads that trace directly. R57 announces 12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks and sits at card 0.748 against dense 0.385; R52 names five datasets including ImageNet and Cityscapes at card 0.679 against dense 0.402; R31 names a TPUv3 Pod, batch size 32868 and BERT-scale training at card 0.534 while dense puts it at 0.979; R39 leans on extensive experiments on multiple environments at card 0.568 against dense 0.291. Tagged mixed, and honestly so: resource-rich groups can both buy breadth AND do better work, and this channel cannot separate the two.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional compute resources and team size

proposals.name: Skim-optimised layout: punchline first, headline number last
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the text is arranged for a fast skim. Score four placement features: (i) the central claim or contribution appears within the first two sentences rather than after extended background; (ii) explicit signposting connectives are used (First, Second, Finally, our contributions are, specifically, in contrast); (iii) sentences are short and declarative rather than long and subordinate-clause-heavy; (iv) the final sentence carries a crisp payoff, typically a headline number, a state-of-the-art statement or an artifact link. Anchors: 0 = none of the four, the point emerges late through long clause-chains with no closing payoff; 5 = two of the four; 10 = all four strongly present. Judge LAYOUT AND PLACEMENT ONLY. Never judge whether the content deserves the emphasis it is given, and never treat a background-first or clause-heavy abstract as worse writing.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint, with the receiving side as the ultimate driver: abstracts are read under a severe time budget, and groups that have absorbed this write punchline-first. That packaging skill is taught, not discovered, so it tracks mentorship rather than research content, and it is exactly what a sequential criterion-by-criterion judge finds easiest to satisfy. R57 opens on the open-question framing, signposts with in contrast and as a result, and closes on new state-of-the-art results (card 0.748 vs dense 0.385); R35 closes on a headline 1.046 human-normalised score plus a repository link (card 0.953 vs dense 0.573); R21 closes on 10.9 and 12.4 percent MAE improvements plus a link (card 0.974 vs dense 0.094). The clause-heavy, background-first texts run the other way, R30 (card 0.363 vs dense 0.009) and R05 (card 0.603 vs dense 0.056). Tagged mixed because experienced mentorship plausibly improves the research as well as its packaging.
proposals.upstream_parent: author experience with the review process and mentorship in manuscript packaging

proposals.name: Non-native-English micro-markers and conversion artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of two co-occurring surface families. Family one, second-language micro-markers: missing or superfluous articles (for example we propose novel method; The most GCNs suffer the performance loss), subject-verb or singular-plural disagreement, non-idiomatic collocations and preposition choices, and inconsistent US versus UK spelling within one text. Family two, manuscript-conversion artifacts: unbalanced or TeX-style quotation marks, HTML entities left unrendered in the text (for example k>1), raw Unicode symbols standing where math markup was intended, and stray markup commands. Anchors: 0 = idiomatic prose with no artifacts; 3 = one marker in the whole text; 6 = three or four markers; 10 = several markers in every few sentences. Score FREQUENCY OF THESE SURFACE MARKERS ONLY. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, whether the authors are competent, whether the ideas are clearly expressed, or whether the text looks professional.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. Which language the authors write in natively, and whether anyone copy-edited or cleanly compiled the file, are invisible upstream facts that leave a dense, easily-counted textual residue - and a criterion judge scoring clarity or presentation will absorb that residue whether or not it is asked to. The residue is not aligned with either model here, which is the signature of a nuisance: R47 carries The most GCNs suffer the performance loss and sits card 0.218 against dense 0.618; R01 carries we propose novel method and sits card 0.479 against dense 0.179; R11 leaves an unbalanced quote in the noise mode and sits card 0.436 against dense 0.838; and R14 leaves a raw HTML entity k>1 in the text yet is the second-highest card row in the slice at 0.923. Tagged not-mixed: a producer first language does not cause research quality, and this channel must be discounted rather than banded.
proposals.upstream_parent: author first-language background and access to copy-editing or submission tooling

proposals.name: Technical-era vintage of the vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the text is anchored to an OLDER technical era rather than the most recent one, judged from vocabulary alone. Cues: named datasets and benchmarks (older end - MNIST, CIFAR-10, GTSRB, PASCAL-style 2D bounding boxes, MuJoCo, Atari, GLUE; recent end - nuScenes, Argoverse, NTU-120, PKU-MMD, Atari 100k, ImageNet-scale transformer suites); named models and methods (older end - SVM, VGG perceptual loss, LSTM, ResNet, BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT; recent end - vision transformers, world models, neural fields and coordinate networks, hyperbolic and spectral self-supervision); hardware and framing conventions of the period. Anchors: 0 = vocabulary is entirely of the most recent era visible in this corpus; 5 = a mix, or era-neutral formal language with no dateable nouns; 10 = vocabulary is entirely of the oldest era visible in this corpus. Score ERA PLACEMENT ONLY. Neither era is better; do not judge whether the work is dated, timely, or superseded, and do not judge whether the benchmarks chosen were the right ones.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint. The submission year is an unseen upstream fact that determines what a text can possibly mention, and it leaves an extremely legible lexical trace. It matters here because the two models are dated differently: the dense reader ranks era-old, widely-echoed formulations very high while the criterion bank, whose items encode current expectations about ablations, released code and quantified deltas, does not - R07 (Gumbel-Softmax era vocabulary, dense 0.880 vs card 0.598), R31 (LARS, BERT, TPUv3 Pod, dense 0.979 vs card 0.534), R32 (dense 0.991 vs card 0.299), R43 (dense 0.904 vs card 0.419), R45 (dense 0.925 vs card 0.274). The oldest row in the slice, R49, written in pre-deep-learning object-class-model vocabulary, runs the other way at dense 0.105 vs card 0.410, and the most recent rows R35 (card 0.953) and R51 (card 0.910) sit card-high. Tagged mixed because methodological standards genuinely rise over time, so era is entangled with real rigour.
proposals.upstream_parent: calendar date of production and submission cycle

proposals.name: Decisiveness of the central claim
proposals.instruction: Score how decisively and unhedgedly the abstract states its main empirical or theoretical finding. A 10 is a single, confidently stated result with no qualifying language ('X is optimal', 'X eliminates the need for Y', 'X consistently outperforms'). A 0 is a claim buried in qualifiers and partial wins ('comparable to', 'more than competitive', 'underperforms in one case but surpasses in others', 'promising despite').
proposals.rationale: Explains splits where confident single-result papers rank high with the dense model (e.g., R28's clean 'orders of magnitude more efficient... comparably accurate' claim, R36's unhedged negative finding) while abstracts that hedge across multiple partial wins are pulled up by the scorecard despite dense skepticism (e.g., R13's 'comparable or higher sample efficiency', R35's '2 out of 3 downstream tasks').

proposals.name: Concrete numeric result density
proposals.instruction: Score how many specific, checkable numeric results (percentages, deltas, counts, timings) the abstract reports, independent of how positive or well-supported they are. A 10 packs multiple precise figures (e.g., '10.9% improvement', '5-fold reduction', '76 minutes'). A 0 reports only qualitative adjectives ('significant', 'considerable', 'remarkable') with no numbers at all.
proposals.rationale: Rows like R60 (10.9%/12.4% MAE improvement) and R41 (5-fold/2-fold/4x speedups) sit in the dense_low_card_high half despite the underlying contribution being narrow engineering work, suggesting the scorecard is drawn to numeric specificity as a rigor proxy even when dense judges the overall contribution as modest.

proposals.name: Claimed generality beyond the motivating case
proposals.instruction: Score how broadly the abstract frames the intended scope of applicability of its core idea. A 10 explicitly frames the contribution as a general-purpose tool/technique usable across multiple distinct tasks or domains. A 0 frames the work as solving one narrow, specific case (a single species, a single dataset, a single narrowly-scoped application) with no claim of broader applicability.
proposals.rationale: R01 (Gumbel-Softmax) is explicitly framed as applicable to 'structured output prediction and unsupervised generative modeling tasks... semi-supervised classification' and sits dense_high_card_low, whereas R21's zebrafish swim-bout classifier is framed around one specific biological example and sits dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Causal diagnosis precedes the fix
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly names the specific mechanism(s) that cause an existing method to fail, before presenting a solution matched to that diagnosis. A 10 enumerates specific causal reason(s) for the failure and shows the proposed fix addresses each one directly. A 0 proposes a method without ever explaining why prior approaches fall short.
proposals.rationale: R48 explicitly enumerates two causes of knowledge-distillation failure on object detection and matches two techniques to them; R30 explicitly targets 'shortcomings' in the current theoretical account of double descent. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense is sensitive to this diagnose-before-fix structure that a criterion-by-criterion scorecard may not weight as heavily.

proposals.name: Novelty of the core technical mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's central contribution is a genuinely new algorithmic/mathematical mechanism versus an application or recombination of already-established mechanisms to a new setting. A 10 introduces a mechanism that did not exist before (a new estimator, a new distribution, a new operator). A 0 applies a well-known mechanism (attention, GANs, distillation, ensembling) to a new domain without altering the mechanism itself.
proposals.rationale: R01 introduces a genuinely new Gumbel-Softmax distribution and gradient estimator (dense_high_card_low), while R08 applies the existing self-attention mechanism across network layers (dense_low_card_high) -- same broad category of contribution, but only one invents new machinery.

proposals.name: Single-idea compressibility (elegance)
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper's core contribution can be stated as one simple, memorable idea versus a bundle of several loosely-related components. A 10 is a paper whose whole contribution reduces to one clean sentence. A 0 requires listing several separate components/mechanisms (i, ii, iii) to describe what was actually done.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('fix the last classifier layer instead of training it') is a single elegant idea and is dense_high_card_low; R39 (PAPO) requires three named components -- encoding, hypernetwork, and size-as-input -- to describe, and is dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Enumerated breadth of empirical validation
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the abstract enumerates the number/names of datasets, baselines, tasks, or settings used to validate the method. A 10 lists a specific count or roster (e.g., '12 baselines, 16 search spaces, 86 datasets', or datasets named individually). A 0 refers to validation only in general terms ('extensive experiments', 'a range of tasks') without naming or counting anything.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks') and R32 (five datasets individually named: CIFAR, SVHN, STL-10, ImageNet, Cityscapes) are both dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this checklist-completeness signal more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Candor about partial or mixed results
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract honestly discloses partial wins, losses, or mixed performance rather than presenting uniformly positive results. A 10 explicitly states where the method underperforms or only partially succeeds. A 0 reports only uniform success with no acknowledged weak points.
proposals.rationale: R05 explicitly admits the method 'underperforms one of the benchmarks in a single game' while winning others, and R35 reports SOTA on one dataset but only '2 out of 3' on another -- both dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard credits this candor as rigor while dense discounts the overall weaker result package.

proposals.name: Explicit code/artifact release mention
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly states that code, models, or data will be or are publicly released. A 10 states a concrete release (e.g., a GitHub link or explicit 'code is available'). A 0 makes no mention of release or reproducibility artifacts.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('Open code for reproducing and extending our results is provided') and R60 ('Code is available at https://github.com/...') both make explicit release statements and both are dense_low_card_high, with R60 among the largest dense/scorecard gaps in the whole slice -- suggesting the scorecard treats a release statement as a quality proxy that dense does not reward.

proposals.name: Plain-language translation of technical significance
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract translates its technical mechanism into an intuitive, plain-language statement of why it matters, versus staying entirely inside unexplained specialist notation and jargon. A 10 gives an accessible analogy or plain-language 'so what' alongside the technical content. A 0 is a wall of unexplained domain-specific terminology (e.g., named theorems, algebraic structures) with no plain-language grounding of significance.
proposals.rationale: R42 stays entirely in specialist control-theory/Lie-algebra language throughout and has the single lowest dense_pct of the entire slice, while R55 grounds its (also fairly technical) idea in an accessible neuroscience analogy ('grandmother cells') and is dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Named, precise comparison to specific prior methods
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract names specific prior competing methods and states precisely the axis along which the new method wins or loses against them, versus comparing only to an unnamed generic 'baselines' or 'state of the art'. A 10 names a specific prior method and gives a precise, qualified comparison (e.g., 'X performs poorly for Y, unlike Z'). A 0 only says it 'outperforms baselines' or 'the state of the art' with no method named.
proposals.rationale: R49 names LARS specifically and precisely qualifies where it fails ('LARS performs poorly for attention models like BERT'), and R03 names and critiques 'accuracy-based approaches' as inconsistent -- both dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense rewards this kind of scholarly precision.

proposals.name: Rhetorical framing as adjudicating a field debate
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly frames itself as resolving an open question or tension in prior literature, using a direct question or an explicit 'prior work suggests X, but...' setup, versus simply stating 'we propose method M for task T' without any such framing device. A 10 opens with an explicit posed question or named tension the paper will resolve. A 0 states its contribution directly with no debate-framing device.
proposals.rationale: R07 opens with 'a recent line of...results has corroborated a widely observed phenomenon...however, is random optimal?' and R54 frames itself as identifying 'potential hazards' in a standard approach -- both dense_low_card_high, suggesting this structural rhetorical device is something a criterion-based scorecard rewards more than the dense reader.

proposals.name: Economy of exposition (information per sentence)
proposals.instruction: Score how much distinct information each sentence of the abstract carries, independent of topic. A 10 is a short, tight abstract where every sentence adds new, non-redundant content. A 0 is a long abstract that restates the same point multiple ways or pads with generic filler sentences.
proposals.rationale: R50 (3 short sentences) and R25 (compact, direct) are the two highest dense_pct rows in the entire 60-item slice, both dense_high_card_low, while longer, more diffusely structured abstracts such as R39 sit dense_low_card_high -- suggesting the dense model rewards terse density that a scorecard, reading criterion by criterion, may not specifically credit.

proposals.name: Challenges a widely-held assumption or standard practice
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly overturns or complicates a piece of received wisdom or standard practice in the field, versus simply extending or applying accepted practice without challenging any assumption. A 10 states a finding that directly contradicts what practitioners would expect (e.g., a standard component turns out to be unnecessary, or a technique backfires). A 0 straightforwardly builds on accepted assumptions without surprising anyone.
proposals.rationale: R51 shows the standard practice of training the final classifier layer is largely unnecessary, and R36 shows GNN structure-aware perturbations can make a model perform worse than an ignorant baseline -- both are dense_high_card_low and both directly upend a standard expectation.

proposals.name: Explicit formal proof/derivation language for central claims
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract uses explicit formal-proof or derivation verbs ('we prove', 'we derive', 'we give a theoretical proof') to support its central claim, versus relying solely on empirical/experimental demonstration language ('experiments show', 'we demonstrate'). A 10 states a central claim is formally proven or derived. A 0 supports every claim only through described experiments, with no proof or derivation language.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('We prove that the KL divergence between stochastic processes equals...') and R29 ('We give theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative') both use explicit proof language and both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense responds to this formal-guarantee framing distinctly from purely empirical result claims.

proposals.name: Rhetorical-slot completeness: motivation, method, experiment, result
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how many of the four standard abstract components -- (1) a problem/motivation statement, (2) a description of the proposed method, (3) a description of the experimental setup, and (4) reported results -- are explicitly and clearly present in the text. Score 0 if the text is a bare title or a single vague sentence with none of these components spelled out, and 10 if all four components are explicitly and fully present. Do NOT judge whether the motivation is compelling, the method is sound, or the results are good -- score only whether each component is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R06 has literally no abstract body beyond its title (dense_pct=.521, card_pct=.192) and R59 is a two-sentence abstract with no motivation paragraph or reported numbers (dense_pct=.996, card_pct=.321); both are extreme dense_high_card_low cases where a checklist-style scorecard has almost nothing to grade against, unlike R20 and R29, which spell out motivation, method, experiments, and results in full (both dense_low_card_high, card_pct=.974 and .568).

proposals.name: Density of specific numeric results reported
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how many distinct specific numeric results appear in the text (e.g., percentages, parameter counts, FLOPs, speedup factors, dataset sizes, benchmark scores). Score 0 if no numbers of this kind appear anywhere, and 10 if many distinct numeric claims are packed into the text. Do NOT judge whether the numbers are impressive, correct, or meaningful -- score only how many such numeric claims are textually present.
proposals.rationale: R20 packs in '10.9% and 12.4% improvement in Mean Absolute Error' plus a code link (dense_pct=.094, card_pct=.974) and R32 stacks six separate percentage figures (40%, 0.5%, 2.8%, 43%, 0.8%, 3%; dense_pct=.372, card_pct=.923), both extreme dense_low_card_high cases, while R03 and R13 report their findings purely qualitatively with zero numeric claims (dense_pct=.427/.303, card_pct=.047/.034, both dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Explicit itemized contribution scaffolding (First/Second/Finally)
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much the text uses explicit enumerative rhetorical scaffolding to lay out its contributions or steps -- phrases like 'First,', 'Second,', 'Next,', 'Finally,', 'two-fold', 'three-fold', or numbered claims. Score 0 if there is no such ordinal/enumerative scaffolding anywhere, and 10 if the text is heavily structured with multiple explicit ordinal markers. Do NOT judge whether the listed contributions themselves are good or important -- score only the presence of this rhetorical scaffolding.
proposals.rationale: R28 uses 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...' to walk through four claims (dense_pct=.154, card_pct=.628) and R29 announces 'Our contributions are three-fold. First, ... Next, ... Finally, ...' (dense_pct=.291, card_pct=.568); R39 similarly opens with 'Our contribution is two-fold. First, ... Second, ...' (dense_pct=.081, card_pct=.376) -- all three are dense_low_card_high, suggesting this templated scaffolding (plausibly coached or house-style writing) is legible to a criterion-by-criterion scorecard judge in a way it is not to a dense reader.

proposals.name: Explicit code or artifact release statement
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how explicitly the text states that code, data, or pretrained models are or will be publicly released (e.g., a GitHub/project URL, or an explicit sentence promising release). Score 0 if there is no such statement anywhere, and 10 if there is an explicit, unambiguous release statement (ideally with a link). Do NOT judge whether releasing the artifact was a good practice or whether the artifact is actually useful -- score only whether the release statement is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R05 ends with 'Our code is available at https://github.com/...' (dense_pct=.568, card_pct=.868), R24 states 'Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available at ...' (dense_pct=.214, card_pct=.731), and R51 promises 'we release our code and models at ...' (dense_pct=.573, card_pct=.953) -- all dense_low_card_high -- while R01 and R03, both dense_high_card_low, contain no release statement at all (dense_pct=.987/.427, card_pct=.444/.047).

proposals.name: Density of formal mathematical/symbolic notation
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much specialized mathematical/symbolic notation appears (inline formulas, Greek letters, subscripts/superscripts, big-O/tilde-O expressions, set/space notation like R^d). Score 0 if the text is plain prose with no symbolic notation, and 10 if the text is dense with symbolic expressions throughout. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is correct, rigorous, or important -- score only how much symbolic notation is visibly present in the text.
proposals.rationale: R48 is thick with expressions like 'epsilon-coreset of size O(m + poly(k eps^{-1}))' (dense_pct=.474, card_pct=.030) and R54 reports a bound 'O~(d^2 H^5 / eps^2)' (dense_pct=.278, card_pct=.004) -- both dense_high_card_low with near-floor card percentiles -- whereas prose-only, notation-free abstracts like R05 and R25 (both dense_low_card_high) contain no inline formulas at all.

proposals.name: Extent of adversarial/security-threat subject framing
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much the abstract centers on adversarial/security-threat framing -- attacks, adversarial examples, backdoors, poisoning, defenses, robustness certificates against a malicious actor. Score 0 if the topic has nothing to do with adversarial/security framing, and 10 if the entire abstract is organized around an attack-or-defense narrative. Do NOT judge whether this is an important or trendy topic to work on -- score only how much of the text is organized around this specific subject-matter framing.
proposals.rationale: Seven of the dense_high_card_low rows in this slice are built around explicit attack/defense framing: R01 ('adversarial distortions', 'adversarial accuracy'), R26 ('Stochastic Activation Pruning for Robust Adversarial Defense'), R31 ('WaNet - Imperceptible Warping-based Backdoor Attack'), plus R12, R34, R44, and R53 -- none of this reflects the actual technical quality of the contribution, just a shared subject-matter cluster the dense model happens to rank high and the scorecard does not.

proposals.name: Catchy or informal title phrasing
proposals.instruction: Read the title only (as given at the top of the item text). Rate 0-10 how catchy, informal, or attention-grabbing the title's phrasing is -- e.g., a concrete striking number, a colloquial phrase, an informal self-assessment, or a play on words -- as opposed to a plain technical/descriptive label. Score 0 for a purely technical, neutral, descriptive title, and 10 for a highly memorable/informal hook. Do NOT judge whether the title accurately reflects a good contribution -- score only the rhetorical style of the phrasing.
proposals.rationale: R41's title advertises 'Training BERT in 76 minutes' as a concrete hook (dense_pct=.979, card_pct=.534), R52's title literally calls its own method 'A Very Good Method for Bayes-Adaptive Deep RL' (dense_pct=.778, card_pct=.380), and R59's title 'Logic and the 2-Simplicial Transformer' pairs an evocative name with a two-sentence abstract (dense_pct=.996, card_pct=.321) -- all three are dense_high_card_low, suggesting title flourish tracks the dense model's preference independent of the underlying work.

proposals.name: Hedged vs. confident epistemic phrasing
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much the text uses hedged, tentative epistemic phrasing (e.g., 'we hypothesize', 'may', 'we believe', a rhetorical question posed about the paper's own premise) versus confident, unhedged declarative claims (e.g., 'we prove', 'we show', 'we demonstrate'). Score 0 if the phrasing is entirely confident/declarative throughout, and 10 if the phrasing is heavily hedged/tentative throughout. Do NOT judge whether the underlying claims are actually correct or well-supported -- score only the degree of hedging in the phrasing itself.
proposals.rationale: R33 opens with 'We hypothesise that this property may be problematic' and keeps a tentative register throughout (dense_pct=.132, card_pct=.406) and R09's title itself is a hedged question, 'Is Random Optimal?', repeated as 'However, is random optimal?' in the body (dense_pct=.056, card_pct=.603) -- both dense_low_card_high -- while R04 asserts flatly 'We give theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative' with no hedging (dense_pct=.406, card_pct=.120, dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Density of named prior-method/author citations
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much the text names specific prior methods, algorithms, or authors by name (e.g., a named baseline algorithm, 'X et al. (year)', a specific named hardware/compute platform) rather than referring to prior work only in generic terms ('recent work', 'existing methods'). Score 0 if no specific prior method/author/platform is named anywhere, and 10 if multiple specific named entities are referenced. Do NOT judge whether the comparison to prior work is fair or complete -- score only how many specific named entities appear in the text.
proposals.rationale: R41 names the specific rival algorithm 'LARS' and the specific hardware 'TPUv3 Pod' it was run on (dense_pct=.979, card_pct=.534) and R22 opens by naming 'graph convolutional networks (GCN) recently proposed by Kipf and Welling' (dense_pct=.904, card_pct=.419) -- both dense_high_card_low -- reflecting a level of named engagement with the field's specific artifacts and infrastructure that a generic reference to 'existing methods' would not.
proposals.upstream_parent: community embeddedness / access to comparison infrastructure

proposals.name: Explicit first-to-achieve priority claims
proposals.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how strongly the text makes an explicit claim to being first, novel-in-priority, or unprecedented (e.g., 'we are the first to...', 'for the first time', 'to the best of our knowledge, ... is the first'). Score 0 if no such priority claim appears, and 10 if the text makes an emphatic, explicit priority claim. Do NOT judge whether the priority claim is actually true or historically accurate -- score only whether this rhetorical claim is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R01 states it can 'determine for the first time the exact adversarial accuracy of an MNIST classifier' (dense_pct=.987, card_pct=.444) and R54 states 'To the best of our knowledge, our approach is the first to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence ... at the same time' (dense_pct=.278, card_pct=.004, the lowest card_pct in the entire slice) -- both dense_high_card_low, suggesting explicit priority-claim rhetoric tracks the dense model's preference independent of whether the priority claim is itself substantiated.

proposals.name: Mechanism–Failure Fit
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the central operation directly targets a precisely described failure mode and every major component follows from it; give 0 when the method is generic or mismatched to the stated problem.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R13 tightly connect their interventions to adversarial vulnerability and spatial difficulty, a conceptual fit that surface-level criteria may miss.

proposals.name: Boundary-Condition Specificity
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract states meaningful assumptions, limiting cases, and conditions under which the method changes behavior; give 0 when it makes broad claims without specifying where they apply.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R44 expose conditions under which familiar approaches fail, whereas many dense-low/card-high abstracts foreground formal claims without equally sharp scope boundaries.

proposals.name: Theory-to-Algorithm Closure
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when theoretical analysis directly determines an implementable construction, estimator, or guarantee; give 0 when theory is disconnected from the proposed procedure.
proposals.rationale: R15, R30, and R50 each turn technical analysis into a concrete algorithmic design, a connection often under-credited by fixed criteria.

proposals.name: Explanatory Depth
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract explains why each major design choice is needed and how it changes the computation or inductive bias; give 0 when it mainly names modules or inspirations without an explanatory chain.
proposals.rationale: R31 and R57 describe recognizable architectural additions but provide less mechanism-level explanation than dense-high abstracts such as R05 and R50.

proposals.name: Coupled-Component Necessity
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when interacting components jointly address dependencies in the problem and removing one would undermine the logic of the design; give 0 when components are merely stacked without explaining their interaction.
proposals.rationale: R20, R22, and R28 explicitly coordinate multiple mechanisms around state distributions, future relations, or information preservation.

proposals.name: Confound Discovery and Repair
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete shortcut, artifact, or confound and describes a targeted diagnostic or correction; give 0 when it assumes the observed signal is valid without checking.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R39 make spurious signals central to their methodology, revealing a quality dimension absent from purely method-and-benchmark descriptions.

proposals.name: Construct Operationalization
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when an abstract concept is converted into a precise measurable, optimizable, or testable object tied to the method; give 0 when it remains a slogan or informal motivation.
proposals.rationale: R07, R46, and R48 operationalize graph invariance, perturbation quality, and topology through explicit mathematical objects.

proposals.name: Resource Accounting
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when computational, memory, latency, or deployment constraints are quantified and handled by the core design; give 0 when efficiency is asserted only in general terms.
proposals.rationale: R11, R25, and R40 integrate parallelism, latency, and complexity reductions into their technical contributions rather than treating efficiency as an afterthought.

proposals.name: Abstraction-Level Transferability
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the core abstraction is explicitly reusable across architectures, tasks, or settings with a reason for that reuse; give 0 when portability is merely asserted or narrowly tuned.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R52 illustrate reusable evaluation or encoding abstractions, while R21 and R57 rely more heavily on broad empirical coverage than on a clearly portable principle.

proposals.name: Multiplicity Modeling
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the method represents multiple valid solutions, futures, or explanations without collapsing them into one target; give 0 when an inherently ambiguous problem is forced into a single answer.
proposals.rationale: R22 and R35 directly address stochastic futures and one-of-many solutions, dimensions that standard criteria can over-credit without examining modeling adequacy.

proposals.name: Threat-Model Realism
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when perturbations or failures are constrained to plausible real-world mechanisms and cover the relevant attacker or shift capabilities; give 0 when the threat model is arbitrary, toy-like, or weakly justified.
proposals.rationale: R18, R19, and R42 connect graph, visual, and textual attacks to concrete constraints such as transferability, imperceptibility, or fluency.

proposals.name: Semantic Interpretability
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when learned representations or operators correspond to meaningful domain concepts and the abstract explains that correspondence; give 0 when interpretability is claimed without a semantic mapping.
proposals.rationale: R01, R23, and R39 connect representations to wavelet structures, visual concepts, or interpretable evidence regions.

proposals.name: Reproducibility Specificity
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract specifies datasets, task settings, comparison protocol, essential implementation details, and artifact availability; give 0 when it offers only generic experimental assurances.
proposals.rationale: R29, R33, and R46 provide unusually concrete datasets, implementation resources, or configuration details, exposing a dimension not captured by novelty language alone.

proposals.name: Causal Component Isolation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when controlled interventions or ablations isolate the role of each major component and distinguish it from confounds; give 0 when only the complete system is described.
proposals.rationale: R26, R39, and R59 use fixing, artifact removal, or loss removal to isolate what drives the method's behavior.

proposals.name: Parsimonious Functional Design
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when a small, clearly motivated change supplies substantial functionality with little added machinery; give 0 when complexity accumulates without explaining why each addition is necessary.
proposals.rationale: R08, R26, and R59 emphasize simple architectures or reduced supervision while retaining rich functionality, a form of elegance that generic component counts miss.

proposals.name: Coined Acronym Load
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract introduce or repeatedly use coined acronyms and named method labels? Score only their visible presence, not whether the methods are good.
proposals.rationale: Dense naming is a memorable stylistic signal independent of research quality. Examples include NeRN in R01, TextGrad in R04, HYSP in R14, and MRLA in R50.

proposals.name: Notation Density
proposals.instruction: How much mathematical notation, symbolic variables, equations, asymptotic expressions, or formal operators appear in the abstract? Score only notation prevalence, not technical merit.
proposals.rationale: Formal notation can create an impression of technical sophistication without establishing quality. It is especially visible in R03, R10, R22, and R59.

proposals.name: Quantitative Result Saturation
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract contain numerical results, percentages, counts, speedups, dataset totals, or explicit metric comparisons? Score only the amount of numerical reporting, not whether results are strong.
proposals.rationale: Dense numerical reporting can make an abstract seem concrete and decisive independently of research quality. Examples include R02, R24, R42, and R57.

proposals.name: Artifact Release Signaling
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract advertise code, pretrained models, configurations, datasets, or repository links? Score only visible artifact signaling, not artifact usefulness or research quality.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced groups may more readily release artifacts, and resources may also support genuine quality, making this a mixed nuisance. Visible examples occur in R08, R14, R22, and R34.

proposals.name: Publication-Polish Fluency
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract exhibit highly polished grammar, smooth transitions, standardized abstract structure, and publication-template fluency? Score only surface editing quality, not research quality.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing can improve perceived clarity without changing the underlying research. Strongly conventional, polished presentation is visible in R24, R29, R40, and R42.

proposals.name: Trend-Aligned Vocabulary
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use recognizable fashionable terminology associated with currently prominent machine-learning themes? Score only the presence of trend vocabulary, not whether the topic is important or good.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can influence which topical labels and framing terms appear, without affecting research quality. Examples include robustness language in R04, world-model language in R24, and spectral-augmentation language in R52.

proposals.name: Canonical Ecosystem Naming
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract name canonical datasets, benchmarks, architectures, standard methods, or well-known prior authors? Score only visible ecosystem references, not the importance of the work.
proposals.rationale: Network access and institutional resources can shape familiarity with recognizable benchmarks and communities, while also plausibly supporting genuine quality. Examples include R02, R15, R37, and R57.

proposals.name: Superlative Claim Rhetoric
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract use superlatives, priority claims, novelty claims, or emphatic comparative language such as first, novel, superior, remarkable, or state of the art? Score only rhetorical frequency, not truth or quality.
proposals.rationale: Promotional claim density can influence reader salience without demonstrating research quality. It appears repeatedly in R10, R24, R42, and R60.

proposals.name: Title-Level Branding
proposals.instruction: How much does the title use slogans, puns, imperatives, evaluative adjectives, or highly branded method phrasing? Score only title construction, not whether the paper is good.
proposals.rationale: Attention-oriented titles can affect memorability independently of substance. Examples include “You Only Need” in R60, “A Very Good Method” in R46, and “Simple” in R56.

proposals.name: Deployment-Impact Framing
proposals.instruction: How much does the abstract frame the work around deployment, practical usefulness, computational cost, trustworthiness, scalability, or end-user impact? Score only framing extent, not practical or scientific quality.
proposals.rationale: Organizational incentives can encourage application-oriented framing and can also provide resources that improve genuine work, so this is mixed. Such framing is visible in R02, R10, R42, R49, and R58.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Problem Diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and designs the method directly to address it; score 0 when it only states a generic problem and adds an unexplained technique.
proposals.rationale: Motivated by the causal account of spurious features and targeted counterfactual data in R01, the optimization-specific diagnosis in R04, and the loss pathology analyzed in R44.

proposals.name: Theory-to-Algorithm Translation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a formal result is clearly converted into a practical algorithm, objective, estimator, or guarantee; score 0 when theory and method are merely adjacent claims.
proposals.rationale: R05 turns stochastic-process KL theory into a finite-measurement training objective, while R20 converts experiment-design theory into a deployment-efficient RL algorithm.

proposals.name: Realistic Stress-Test Coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation deliberately includes difficult, varied, or realistic failure conditions matching the claimed challenge; score 0 when evaluation uses only routine settings unrelated to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R02 tests stealth against humans, machine defenses, and multiple datasets; R59 spans real-world perturbation types, scales, and adversarial corruption settings.

proposals.name: Scalable Efficiency With Preserved Function
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a concrete efficiency gain, explains its algorithmic source, and states what capability is preserved; score 0 when efficiency is asserted without mechanism or capability comparison.
proposals.rationale: R07 links large-batch optimization to a dramatic training-time reduction without degradation, while R47 derives lower-complexity equivariant layers while preserving expressiveness.

proposals.name: Structure-Aligned Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method encodes a domain structure or invariance that is explicitly connected to the task and empirically examined; score 0 when architectural structure is arbitrary or purely cosmetic.
proposals.rationale: R13 connects spectral filters to local and global graph context, and R60 derives graph augmentation from spectral structure rather than uniform random perturbations.

proposals.name: Threat-Model Evaluation Completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies the adversary or verifier access, perturbation class, and complementary attack or certification procedures; score 0 when robustness is claimed against an unspecified threat.
proposals.rationale: R26 combines exact verification with adversarial-example search, while R57 explicitly defines loss-oracle black-box access and incorporates query-efficient priors.

proposals.name: Boundary and Failure Characterization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract distinguishes regimes where the method helps, does not help, or changes behavior, with explicit assumptions; score 0 when it presents only universal-sounding success claims.
proposals.rationale: R12 characterizes when random permutations are or are not optimal, and R46 analyzes how finite width and loss choice affect double descent.

proposals.name: Causal Component Ablation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract isolates multiple failure sources and assigns each a targeted component whose role is separately motivated or tested; score 0 when the method is an undifferentiated bundle.
proposals.rationale: R43 attributes detection failures to foreground-background imbalance and missing relations, then introduces corresponding distillation mechanisms; R31 identifies artifact reliance and verifies its effect by removal.

proposals.name: Transfer Across Tasks or Domains
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed principle is demonstrated across meaningfully different tasks, domains, or architectures without being narrowly redesigned for each; score 0 when evidence is confined to one tightly matched setting.
proposals.rationale: R10 moves from grid-world uncertainty exploration to MuJoCo meta-RL, while R18 evaluates across several skeleton datasets and downstream action-recognition tasks.

proposals.name: Learning Under Data Scarcity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method directly addresses limited, sparse, imbalanced, or costly data and explains why its design helps; score 0 when data availability is assumed unconstrained.
proposals.rationale: R19 targets ultra-high-resolution inputs under computational limits, and R56 transfers multi-view priors specifically to scarce and imbalanced fine-grained detection data.

proposals.name: Uncertainty Quality and Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is represented at an appropriate level, its failure modes are analyzed, and reliability is evaluated beyond point prediction; score 0 when uncertainty is only named without a reliability argument.
proposals.rationale: R05 uses function-level priors for extrapolation and uncertainty, R15 relocates stochasticity to activations, and R44 exposes unstable heteroscedastic likelihood estimates.

proposals.name: Resource-Aware Method Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when memory, latency, parallelism, or deployment constraints shape the method and are quantitatively evaluated alongside task quality; score 0 when resource claims are incidental or unmeasured.
proposals.rationale: R21 removes sequential SDE integrators for lower-variance parallel learning, while R34 and R41 explicitly target memory footprint, latency, and inference speed.

proposals.name: Compositional Generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly handles combinations of reusable components, agents, views, skills, or solutions and explains how composition remains workable; score 0 when it addresses only isolated cases.
proposals.rationale: R11 composes lower-level policies through learned transition distributions, and R35 conditions policies on population size across related games.

proposals.name: Reproducible Specification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract provides unusually concrete implementation, data, evaluation, or artifact details sufficient to make replication plausible; score 0 when the proposal remains too vague to reconstruct or assess.
proposals.rationale: R07 names a precise batch-size and runtime setting and provides an implementation, while R16 and R59 explicitly offer code, models, configurations, and reproducibility artifacts.

proposals.name: Explanatory Insight Beyond Performance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work yields a transferable conceptual explanation, diagnostic, or unifying interpretation in addition to a method and measurements; score 0 when it reports improvements without illuminating why they occur.
proposals.rationale: R06 reframes representation evaluation through MDL and reveals data-efficiency properties, while R39 unifies several Lipschitz constructions through a common algebraic condition.

proposals.name: Abstract verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of extended prose, clause density, and explanatory detail present; judge only amount of text, not whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R30 contain unusually long, highly detailed abstracts with many successive claims, making verbosity a plausible stylistic nuisance independent of substance.

proposals.name: Mathematical notation density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of equations, symbols, variables, asymptotic notation, and formal mathematical expressions; judge only their visible amount, not their correctness or value.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R28 prominently use asymptotic expressions, parameters, and formal notation, while R36 uses dense mathematical and theoretical terminology. This visible style can affect text processing without being research quality.

proposals.name: Numerical-result density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of precise numerical figures, percentages, counts, time measurements, speedups, or benchmark quantities; judge only the presence of numbers, not their magnitude or significance.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R30 include numerous exact quantities such as durations, dataset counts, batch sizes, and percentage-like measurements. Numerical specificity can act as a persuasive or lexical cue without itself indicating quality.

proposals.name: Artifact-release signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit language promising or linking code, models, datasets, configurations, or other research artifacts; judge only the presence of release signaling, not whether the artifacts are useful or real.
proposals.rationale: R06, R10, R21, and R37 explicitly mention released code, models, configurations, or pretrained weights. Access to infrastructure and release practices may influence both textual reception and genuine research execution, so this is a mixed nuisance.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth listing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the abstract lists many datasets, tasks, domains, architectures, or comparison settings; judge only breadth of enumeration, not comprehensiveness or research quality.
proposals.rationale: R02 enumerates many baselines, search spaces, and datasets, while R42 lists several datasets and application settings. Resources and research networks can enable broad evaluations and may also support genuine quality, making this mixed.

proposals.name: Trend-topic vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of vocabulary associated with fashionable or highly visible machine-learning topics, such as Transformers, self-supervision, world models, adversarial robustness, or backdoors; judge only topical wording, not importance or quality.
proposals.rationale: R04, R06, R38, and R51 use vocabulary tied to prominent contemporary themes. Submission timing and community fashion can leave these lexical traces even when they are unrelated to the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Method-acronym density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of invented method names, capitalized abbreviations, and branded component labels; judge only their frequency and prominence, not whether the names are meaningful or the method is good.
proposals.rationale: R06 uses IRIS, R10 uses SNAS, R19 uses HYSP, and R24 uses PAPO while repeatedly naming components. Community conventions and expertise can shape both this branding style and genuine research quality, so the channel is mixed.

proposals.name: Literature-lineage signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit named methods, authors, dates, historical lineage, or detailed comparisons to prior approaches; judge only the amount of lineage signaling, not citation accuracy or importance.
proposals.rationale: R20 names foundational prior work and R32 names multiple prior frameworks and venues; R49 similarly maps several established approaches. Seniority and network access may affect both this textual footprint and actual research capability.

proposals.name: Contribution scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of standardized abstract structure such as numbered contributions, signposts like first/second/finally, and explicit problem-method-result packaging; judge only structural presence, not clarity or quality.
proposals.rationale: R16 uses an explicit first-through-fourth sequence, while R28 and R59 use highly structured contribution summaries. Editing or templating can produce this footprint without changing the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Promotional assertion density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of assertive promotional wording such as novel, remarkable, superior, extensive, first, only, or significant; judge only the frequency of such wording, not whether the assertions are true.
proposals.rationale: R02, R26, R39, and R47 contain repeated emphatic and comparative assertions. Such wording is a surface rhetorical habit that can influence text reception while providing no independent evidence of research quality.
